title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
description:
# Binary Number with Alternating Bits

Given a positive integer `n`, return `true` if every pair of adjacent bits in its binary representation has different values. Otherwise, return `false`.

For example, `5` is `101` in binary, so it has alternating bits. `7` is `111`, so it does not.

Leading zeroes are not part of the binary representation. A single-bit number such as `1` is considered alternating because it has no adjacent pair that can violate the rule.

## Example 1:

**Input:** n = 5
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** The binary representation of 5 is `101`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** n = 7
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The binary representation of 7 is `111`.

## Example 3:

**Input:** n = 11
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The binary representation of 11 is `1011`, whose final two bits are both `1`.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1`

solutions.name: Shift-XOR All-Ones Mask
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute `mask = n ^ (n >> 1)`. If adjacent bits in `n` always differ, then every bit in `mask` below the most significant bit becomes `1`. A number of the form `111...111` satisfies `(mask & (mask + 1)) == 0`.

## Key Insight

XOR reports whether two bits differ. Shifting `n` right by one aligns every bit with its left neighbor, so alternating input becomes an all-ones mask.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Two-Bit Window Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Repeatedly look at the lowest two bits using `n & 3`. The only valid adjacent pairs are `01` and `10`; pairs `00` and `11` violate the alternating rule. Shift right by one to slide the two-bit window.

## Key Insight

Alternation is a local property. Every adjacent pair must be different, so checking all overlapping two-bit windows is enough.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Generate Alternating Target
solutions.description:
## Approach

Generate the only alternating number for each bit length: `1`, `10`, `101`, `1010`, and so on. Stop when the generated pattern is at least `n`, then compare it with `n`.

## Key Insight

Because leading zeroes do not count, there is exactly one alternating binary value for each positive bit length: it must start with `1` and then flip every following bit. Before shifting, guard against passing the positive `int` range so large non-alternating values cannot make the generator overflow and loop forever.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Binary String Adjacent Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Convert `n` to a binary string and compare each character with the previous one. Return `false` as soon as two adjacent characters match.

## Key Insight

This is the most direct translation of the statement. It is less memory efficient than bit operations, but it makes the definition easy to inspect before optimizing.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)

solutions.name: Recursive Adjacent Pair Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Check the lowest adjacent pair. If those two bits are equal, return `false`; otherwise recurse on `n >> 1`, which removes the lowest bit and exposes the next adjacent pair.

## Key Insight

Each recursive call proves one local adjacency and reduces the problem to the remaining prefix. The base case is any single-bit number.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n) for the recursion stack

tests.description: A single bit is vacuously alternating.
Binary 10 is the smallest two-bit alternating value.
Binary 10101 is an odd-length alternating pattern.
Binary 101010 is an even-length alternating pattern.
0x55555555 is the largest positive 31-bit alternating pattern.
One less than the large alternating pattern breaks the low bits.
All low 31 bits set cannot alternate.
